item.title: Circularly polarized luminescence in boron- and nitrogen-embedded helicenes: molecular design, performance benchmarks and device applications
item.description: Boron- and nitrogen-embedded helicenes combine helical chirality with a conjugated B,N-containing backbone. Some multiple-resonance emitters also exhibit narrow emission bands and high photoluminescence quantum yields (Φ). Comparing their circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) requires distinguishing solution, film and device measurements and identifying the electronic transitions that give rise to the absorption and emission dissymmetry factors. We examine four aspects of molecular design and device performance: electronic structure, excitedstate dynamics, transition dipole moments and configurational stability. The review covers 29 B,Ncontaining entries and six classes of controls. We record the medium, physical state and source of each measurement and recalculate CPL brightness as BCPL = εΦ|glum|/2 where all three inputs can be traced. Across 20 compounds with Φ and |glum| measured in the same medium, the correlation is weakly negative (Pearson r = −0.331, Spearman ρ = −0.271) and sensitive to the scaffolds represented. Thirteen entries allow comparison of the dissymmetry factors of corresponding absorption and emission bands in the same medium. Molecular and device benchmarks include |glum| = 0.048 for [10]HAB and a red (M,M)-RBNN device combining a maximum external quantum efficiency of 36.6% with gEL = +1.91 × 10 3. Six pairwise - relationships and nine diagnostic questions distinguish structural interpretations supported by comparisons within a series from those that still require emitting-state transition moments, enantiomeric purity after processing or device measurements at operating luminance.

item.title: Benchmarking Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Plus One Double (TDDFT-1D) for Potential Energy Surfaces
item.description: Time-dependent density functional theory plus one double (TDDFT-1D) improves on conventional TDDFT by including one specially chosen doubly excited electronic configuration. In this study, we evaluate the ability of that method to describe the ground-and excited-state potential energy surfaces (PESs) of selected model compounds relevant to photochemistry. We find that its accuracy is highly dependent on the given test case. For some systems with relatively little multiconfigurational character, the calculated PESs coincide very closely with benchmark data derived from high-level wavefunction-based calculations. In the most favorable cases–methylene and azomethane–and with specific choices of adjustable simulation parameters, TDDFT-1D PESs follow the benchmark data to around 0.2 eV. For some others, the calculated PESs are distorted to a varying degree. In order to pave the way for future studies employing TDDFT-1D, we identify some specific situations where it may potentially fail, and which should be therefore avoided.

item.title: Chemotype-Symmetric Junction-Tree VAE for SARS-CoV-2 Mpro Inhibitor Design
item.description: The main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2 is inhibited by covalent drugs such as nirmatrelvir, whose activity comes from a reactive warhead that bonds to the enzyme. Designing safer analogs of these inhibitors is hard because standard drug-likeness objectives optimise away the very warhead that makes them work, and because the fused-aromatic scaffolds they are built on are where generative models most often produce invalid structures. This work presents a generative framework that improves predicted safety while preserving both the warhead and target affinity. Built on a junction-tree variational autoencoder, it represents each molecule as a tree of chemical fragments, encodes it into a continuous latent space, and generates analogs by decoding new points near a known inhibitor’s latent code. A chemotype-symmetric fragment vocabulary gives uniform coverage across the diverse Mpro inhibitor chemotype classes, and a graph-attention attachment scorer conditioned on the latent code reassembles their edgefused ring chemistry at decoding time, reconstructing 19 of 20 top-active targets faithfully. Over this latent space the framework runs a constrained six-objective search that trades off drug-likeness, synthetic accessibility, warhead retention, predicted potency, lipophilicity, and warhead reversibility. Predicted potency comes from a deep-ensemble bioactivity surrogate, whose disagreement across the ensemble also sets an anchor-relative uncertainty cap that gates the search away from chemistry it has not seen. The optimiser is NSGA-III, selected after benchmarking a catalogue of multi-objective methods on this pipeline. From all twenty anchors, spanning five Mpro inhibitor chemotype classes, the framework produces a de-duplicated library of 1,013 analogs and retains the source warhead in 85% of the parents that carry one. A perwarhead analysis shows predicted mutagenicity is governed by the warhead class rather than by covalency, the reversible nitrile of the marketed inhibitors being as clean as non-covalent chemistry while the irreversible chloroacetamide and Michael warheads carry the liability. The final Pareto front of 138 analogs is predicted as safe as or safer than each analog’s own source inhibitor on four of eight ADMET endpoints and at parity on mutagenicity, with the warhead retained in 94% of the front and docked binding within AutoDock Vina’s scoring error of the parents, at a modest predicted-potency cost. The strongest single candidate is a dual-warhead analog of nirmatrelvir, predicted safer than the drug on seven of eight endpoints. This safety advantage over the source inhibitors, obtained without erasing the warhead, is the central result, and one that objectives penalising the covalent warhead cannot reach without discarding the mechanism.

item.title: Are fungi and their enzymes effective for biodegradable microplastics in wastewater? Linking particle retention to polymer-carbon conversion
item.description: Biodegradable microplastics (BMPs) can persist through wastewater treatment and be transferred from water to sludge without substantial polymer degradation, posing potential risks to aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Fungi can colonize biodegradable polyester particles and produce extracellular enzymes capable of depolymerization, but their effectiveness in continuous municipal wastewater treatment remains uncertain. This critical review examines the relationships among particle retention, fungal enzyme activity, polymer hydrolysis, and the fate of released carbon. We distinguish physical capture from depolymerization, assimilation, and mineralization, drawing on evidence from fungal cultures, isolated enzymes, and mixed microbial systems. Three potential treatment configurations are evaluated: recoverable fungal pellets, attached fungal growth, and enzymatic hydrolysis of concentrated BMP fractions. Their feasibility depends on sustained particle–enzyme contact, catalytic activity under non-sterile conditions, and downstream utilization or recovery of hydrolysis products. We propose evaluation criteria incorporating polymer-specific inventories across effluent, sludge, and retained solids; isotope-based carbon tracing; matched experimental controls; and energy and material accounting. This framework identifies the evidence needed to determine whether fungal interventions achieve genuine reductions in residual polymer discharge rather than merely transferring biodegradable microplastics between environmental compartments.

item.title: Spatial arrangement of bonds governs the thermodynamics of multivalent DNA origami interfaces
item.description: Multivalency, the simultaneous engagement of many weak bonds, underlies recognition between cells, viruses, and proteins and enables assembly of DNA origami into micrometer-scale structures. Predicting the stability of a multivalent interface is difficult because each bond's contribution depends on the number, strength, and arrangement of the other bonds and on the scaffold that presents them, which rarely vary independently. We use DNA origami tiles with 11 addressable sites along one edge to build 236 interfaces in which bond number, strength, and arrangement are set independently, and measure their melting by FRET. Multivalency stabilizes interfaces far beyond any single bond. Once two tiles dock, each further bond finds its partner at an effective concentration about 105-fold above the tile concentration. Stability nevertheless grows subadditively, because only part of an interface melts as one unit and added bonds contribute only insofar as they are formed near the interface melting temperature. Arrangement matters as much as identity: interfaces built from the same bonds lose stability as bonds spread apart, and moving one bond away from two fixed bonds costs 2.5–3 °C per skipped site. A three-parameter multivalent model in which each bond’s effective concentration decays with its distance from the others predicts held-out melting temperatures to within 1.3 °C, outperforming a gradient-boosted regressor. Coarse-grained simulations of polymer-tethered binders reproduce this loss and show that linker and scaffold rigidity set how well binding sites stay in register. These results give design rules and a predictive tool for multicomponent DNA assembly and other multivalent systems.

item.title: Durable Superhydrophobic Surface Engineering for Agricultural and Food-Contact Systems
item.description: Agricultural machinery, storage silos, food-processing pipelines, and packaging substrates operate under harsh coupled mechanical, tribological, chemical, electrochemical, and biological stressors that bare metallic or polymeric bulk materials cannot withstand alone. Engineered superhydrophobic surface–substrate systems—combining controlled micro-/nanoscale topography with low-surface-energy chemistry to sustain a Cassie–Baxter air plastron (static water contact angle θs > 150°, sliding angle α < 10°)—impart emergent wear resistance, corrosion protection, drag reduction, and multi-foulant repulsion across pre-harvest and post-harvest environments. This review examines contemporary surface engineering advances (predominantly 2023–2026) through a process–structure–property lens. Subtractive monolithic texturing (nanosecond/femtosecond laser processing, reactive-ion etching, interference lithography) is critically compared against additive and hybrid deposition routes (nanodiamond composites, sol–gel/mesoporous silica, electrodeposition, electrospinning, cellular armor, and fluorine-free bio-dispersions). Tribological soil/mud anti-adhesion on tillage and harvesting components, electrochemical impedance corrosion protection on magnesium, aluminum, galvanized, and stainless alloys, and turbulent slip hydraulics are evaluated alongside a quantitative cross-study benchmark of bacterial log10 reductions (0.7 to 6.5 log_{10}) separating passive anticontact ceilings from dual-functional synergy. Finally, multiscale surface characterisation, non-destructive examination (plastron tracking, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, X-ray computed tomography), and quality-control protocols for PFAS-free food-contact compliance are established.

item.title: Preserving Identity in an Ecosystem of Synthetic Cells by Inhibiting Fusion with a Macromolecular Crowder
item.description: To synthesize life from non-living matter, we require, at a minimum, ecosystems of synthetic cells that are capable of adaptive evolution. Such evolution, in turn, requires distinct individuals in an ecosystem to compete for resources so that successful ones can pass on their genotypes, while weaker ones succumb. Fuel-dependent synthetic cells built from complex coacervate droplets offer a route towards such evolution: they emerge when fuel is present, decay when it runs out, and freely exchange nutrients and waste with their surroundings. Moreover, because they lack a membrane, they readily take up molecules from their surroundings, negating the need for transmembrane pumps and channels. However, their membrane-less nature comes with downsides—when two droplets collide, they can fuse and pool their contents, erasing the differences between individuals that selection acts on. With a high fusion rate, an ecosystem with many individuals rapidly becomes a homogeneous pool of a few. To overcome that problem, we show that poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), an inert macromolecular crowder, suppresses fusion, allowing synthetic cells with distinct genotypes and phenotypes to coexist and compete within a single population. Crucially, the crowder does not accumulate in the droplets, leaving their interior chemistry untouched. Instead, the crowder reduces how often droplets collide and, more importantly, more than halves the chance that a collision ends in fusion. It does so through a combined effect of reduced interfacial tension and slower diffusion in the surrounding dilute phase, thereby making droplets more resistant to coalescence. For the first time, we can subject an ecosystem of fuel-dependent droplets with individual model identities to multiple fueling-starvation cycles and find that their identity is preserved. We show that crowding agents are a simple, broadly applicable tool for preserving the individual identity of membraneless synthetic cells, a prerequisite for their Darwinian evolution.

item.title: Vicem: Automating Molecular Mechanics Modeling of Solvation Dynamics with Applications to Time-Resolved X-ray Scattering
item.description: Time-resolved X-ray solution scattering (trXSS) probes molecular-scale structural dynamics in solution, but its interpretation requires efficient computational methodologies and models for assessing how changes in solute structure and charge distribution affect the surrounding solvent shell and the resulting scattering signal. We present VICEM, an OpenMM/ASE-based software suite for constructing solvated molecular models, running molecular dynamics simulations, inspecting and analyzing the resulting trajectories, while exposing solute geometry, partial charges, Lennard–Jones parameters, and bonded terms as editable variables for model refinement. VICEM includes an approximate restrained-solute model designed for rapid solvent-shell sampling around prescribed solute geometries, together with utilities for correcting the potential energy along selected intramolecular coordinates. We benchmark the restrained model against established force fields for 244 systems comprising neutral organic molecules, charged organic solutes, and transition-metal complexes. Across 5018 solute-water radial distribution functions, the effect of restraining the solute structure on the solvent shell is generally comparable to differences between established flexible force fields, and diagnostic cases are scrutinized to identify when reference geometry, nonbonded assignment, or suppressed solute flexibility controls the solvent response. For a prototypical iron complex, VICEM is used to scan candidate geometries and quantify the effect of the structure on solvent-shell radial distribution functions and the corresponding scattering signal, showing how VICEM can be used to tune molecular models for structural refinement. VICEM is therefore shown to provide a platform for reproducible solvent-shell modeling and targeted force-field refinement with particular focus on trXSS analysis.

item.title: Gap-weighted diversity space for pool-based molecular screening and why the metric decides whether active learning helps
item.description: Gas-phase density functional theory (DFT) calculations provide valuable electronic structure information for molecular screening but remain computationally expensive for large chemical libraries. At the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) level, screening 8,657 organic carboxylates would require approximately 2.1 × 105 CPU hours. We introduce MolecularLens, an automated computational framework integrating RDKit molecular descriptors, a Monte Carlo dropout Bayesian neural network, a tailored molecular diversity representation (Xcluster), four pool-based acquisition strategies, and Gaussian 16/SLURM workflows. We demonstrate that conventional concatenation of 51 molecular descriptors and 2,048 Morgan fingerprint bits causes fingerprints to dominate approximately 95.5% of squared pairwise distances, potentially biasing diversitybased molecular selection. Xcluster addresses this imbalance through feature compression, targetcorrelation weighting, and controlled feature-block scaling. Using a 3,000-molecule QM9 dataset, we find that informed acquisition strategies consistently underperform random sampling in overall predictive accuracy ((R^2)) but significantly improve recovery of molecules within the lowest 5% of electronic energy gaps. At a 40% sampling budget, hybrid MaxMin recovered 86% of low-gap molecules compared with 35% for random sampling, achieving equivalent recall with approximately 45% fewer DFT calculations. These findings demonstrate that acquisition strategies optimized for targeted molecular discovery can substantially reduce computational costs despite lower aggregate predictive accuracy. We additionally provide a curated library of 8,657 organic carboxylates derived from ChEMBL and identify the importance of robust data validation in automated electronic structure workflows. Overall, MolecularLens provides a framework for computationally efficient, property-directed molecular screening with potential applications in organic energy storage materials.

item.title: Engineering chirality in threaded BODIPYs
item.description: In this article, we explore the possibility of introducing chirality at different structural levels within boron-threaded BODIPYs. Three strategies were investigated, involving a chiral macrocycle, a stereogenic boron center and an axially chiral BODIPY dimer. In the latter case, double threading through boron coordination was achieved for the first time. The optical and chiroptical properties of the three chiral systems were investigated. While the chiral macrocycle leads to the most pronounced chiroptical response with clear evidence of chirality transfer to the BODIPY, all three architectures display measurable electronic circular dichroism and circularly polarized luminescence. These results demonstrate that chirality can be deliberately positioned at distinct structural levels of threaded BODIPYs, providing a modular platform to investigate the interplay between molecular architecture and chiroptical properties.

item.title: Formate and Acetate: A Challenging Case for Microdroplet Chemistry
item.description: Recent studies reported the spontaneous formation of formate and acetate in water microdroplet sprays when exposed to CO2 gas with micromolar yields over timescales of less than seconds. Here, we used in situ Raman spectroscopy of single, optically-trapped water droplets in CO2 gas to investigate whether this unconventional droplet reaction enables product formation on timescales longer than seconds, thus increasing the product yields to amounts potentially providing a competitive green synthesis pathway. The results show that product formation by this droplet reaction does not occur beyond the short timescales reported previously. The present study reveals that single droplets act as extremely sensitive and fast detectors for trace gas amounts of these acids down to the level of parts per trillion. In situ single-droplet Raman spectroscopy offers a fast, sensitive platform for trace gas detection of soluble acids or bases. Single-droplet studies are crucial to advance our knowledge of unusual microdroplet reactivity.

item.title: Kinetic Origin of Limited Chain Growth in CO2-Fischer–Tropsch Synthesis over Cobalt
item.description: Cobalt catalysts selectively produce long-chain hydrocarbons from CO yet convert CO2 almost exclusively to methane. The origin of this selectivity difference remains unclear because CO2 hydrogenation proceeds via a CO intermediate and shares the subsequent reaction network with conventional CO Fischer–Tropsch synthesis. We use a first-principles dual-site microkinetic model to determine why efficient CO2 activation and CH* monomer formation do not result in chain growth. Under CO2 hydrogenation conditions, the model predicts CO2 conversion rates of approximately 10−2 s−1 and almost complete selectivity to methane, in agreement with experiment. CO2 activation on terraces controls the overall rate, whereas CO activation at B5 sites and subsequent CHx hydrogenation control methane formation. Lowering the H2/CO2 ratio decreases the H* coverage but does not induce chain growth, demonstrating that excess surface hydrogen alone does not explain the methane selectivity. Instead, the selectivity is governed by the coverage-dependent kinetic competition between CHx hydrogenation and C–C coupling on the terraces. At CO2 hydrogenation coverages, methanation is kinetically favoured. Near CO saturation, the CO adlayer changes the relative stability of intermediates and transition states, shifting the kinetic balance toward chain growth. However, these high CO* coverages simultaneously inhibit CO2 activation. Coupling cobalt with an ideal reverse water-gas shift function partially decouples both requirements and restores measurable chain growth, but methane remains dominant because the attainable CO partial pressure and H2/CO ratio do not reproduce conventional Fischer–Tropsch conditions. These results reveal a narrow compatibility window between CO2 activation and chain growth and identify functional separation of CO2 activation and hydrocarbon growth as a promising strategy for catalyst design.

item.title: Cooperative OH/CH-based recognition enables lithium chloride binding and extraction
item.description: Lithium chloride is the primary target of ion-pair receptor chemistry aimed at lithium recovery from brines and battery waste. Here, we report the ion-pair receptors for LiCl, built on a resorcinarene scaffold bearing lower-rim CH hydrogen-bond donors, which is crucial for stabilizing the anion in its binding site, combined with OH groups that serve a dual role as anion-binding hydrogen-bond donors as well as Li+ coordination sites. Six receptors were synthesized and structurally characterized by X-ray crystallography: monofunctional control 1, OH-bearing receptors 2-4, ester-functionalized 5, and ether-functionalized 6. NMR titrations in THF-d8 (1H, 7Li) show that receptors 3 and 4 bind LiCl as an ion pair with high avidity (K11K21 ≈ 108-109 M−2), overcoming both the strong competitive solvation of Li+ by THF and the aggregation of LiCl into clusters. DFT modeling of the 4⊃LiCl complex reveals a binding mode in which Cl− is held by aromatic and aliphatic CH groups along with two OH groups, while the Li+ is coordinated by two hydroxyl oxygen atoms and forms a contact ion pair with Cl−. Receptor 3 achieves solid–liquid extraction of LiCl (~34%) into chloroform, outperforming LiNO3 extraction despite the latter's lower lattice energy. Under liquid–liquid extraction (LLE) conditions, receptors 3 and 4 transfer Li+ from water into the green solvent 2-methyltetrahydrofuran (MeTHF), reaching up to 100% receptor saturation and maintaining LiCl extraction abilities in the presence of excess NaCl. These results establish CH/OH-based receptors as a new platform for lithium chloride recognition and extraction from aqueous to ethereal phase.

item.title: First-principles insights into the adsorption of graphene and graphene oxides on anhydrous and hydrated iron oxide
item.description: Density functional theory calculations at the optB88-vdW+U level have been utilised to investigate the adsorption of graphene and graphene oxides with varying degrees of oxidation on anhydrous and hydrated Fe-terminated α−Fe2O3. Unlike idealised functional-group models, the present study considers structurally heterogeneous GO sheets containing hydroxyl and epoxy groups across a realistic range of O:C ratios, together with explicitly hydrated hematite interfaces. Our calculations show that graphene and graphene oxide adsorb via physisorption and chemisorption, respectively. Graphene oxides were found to adsorb more strongly than pristine graphene on hematite in both anhydrous and hydrated conditions. Moreover, we deployed a combination of charge density difference, Bader charge, and crystal orbital Hamilton population analyses to provide both qualitative and quantitative insights into the adsorption mechanisms of graphene and graphene oxides on hematite. Specifically, we reveal that graphene oxides form Fe−O−C interfacial bridges on anhydrous hematite but increasingly complex Fe−O−H· · ·O−C bonds on hydrated surfaces. We further show that the strength and character of interfacial bonding are governed by the accessibility and topology of interfacial bridges, rather than by oxygen content alone. Adsorption therefore reflects a balance between bridge formation, charge redistribution, and the structural deformation of the carbon sheet. Explicit hydration weakens adsorption and changes the relative stability of the interfaces, while different oxidation levels favour distinct bonding configurations and electronic responses. These findings establish hydration state, functional-group distribution, and bridge topology as key design variables for graphene–iron-oxide interfaces, providing mechanistic guidance for tailoring carbon-based materials in tribological, electrochemical, energy-storage, and catalysis applications.

item.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization
item.description: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.

item.title: From Transparent Allenes to Cyanine-like Allylic Cations: Switchable Absorption at the 808 nm Photothermal Window
item.description: Near-infrared (NIR) dyes convert light that penetrates tissue and many materials into heat, the basis of photothermal therapy and of light-driven heating in materials. Most NIR dyes, including cyanines such as indocyanine green (ICG), absorb permanently, so heating cannot be confined to where and when it is wanted. Here, we report tetraaryl allenes that are transparent above 380 nm and become NIR absorbers upon protonation: acid conjugates their two orthogonal diarylmethylene units into 1,1,3,3-tetraarylallyl cations, short polymethine dyes. Base restores the transparent allene. A series of ten derivatives bearing methoxy, diphenylamino (NPh2), and cyano groups shows that the absorption of the cation depends less on the number of donors than on their distribution between the two allyl termini. Two regioisomers that carry the same two NPh2 groups absorb at 742 nm when both sit on one terminus and at 822 nm (ε = 83,000 M–1 cm–1) when one sits on each. Balancing the termini thus lowers the transition energy, raises the absorptivity, and narrows the band. DFT shows the corresponding loss of bond-length and charge asymmetry, as expected on approach to the cyanine limit. Finally, we use this switch for photothermal heating at 808 nm: three different NPh2-containing allylic cations convert absorbed light to heat with η = 52%, three times the value for ICG measured in the same setup, and acid/base cycling switches heating on and off over five cycles.

item.title: How much control is enough? Feed-composition operability and minimum process intervention in CALF-20 CO2/N2 separation
item.description: Adsorption processes rarely see the feed composition used to design their cycles, yet screening and optimisation usually report performance at a single inlet condition. We develop a minimum-control-authority framework for CO2/N2 vacuum swing adsorption with CALF-20, linking literature-derived mixture equilibrium and a published 15% CO2 process anchor to a reduced-order model. For 95% purity and 88% recovery, the frozen cycle is feasible only over 14.19–15.08% inlet CO2; adapting one actuator, or coordinating regeneration pressure and adsorption time, extends the lean boundary to 13.40% and 10.59% (10.95% within assumed equipment limits). At 95% purity and 90% recovery the frozen cycle is infeasible, but adaptation restores operation. Across 205 composition–throughput scenarios, accessible cases rise from 18.0% to 76.6% with two actuators, and a quasi-steady disturbance sequence needs 30% less actuator movement than energy-first re-optimisation. Control authority thus gives a direct measure of process operability, although the boundaries are reduced-order predictions that still need dynamic validation.

item.title: Learning reaction yields across laboratories without sharing data: a benchmark of federated learning with secure aggregation and differential privacy
item.description: Useful reaction data is spread across many laboratories, and most of it is never shared. Federated learning lets labs train one shared model while each lab keeps its own data. This study tests whether that works for predicting reaction yields. Five simulated labs of very different size were built from two public datasets (Buchwald–Hartwig and Suzuki–Miyaura couplings), either sharing the same chemistry or each working on its own substrates. The outcome, in four points. (1) When labs share the same chemistry, the federated model is almost as good as a model trained on all data pooled in one place (R2 0.93 against 0.96), and the smallest lab halves its prediction error. (2) When each lab works on its own substrates, a model trained by one lab fails on other labs' reactions (R2 below 0), while the federated model works (R2 0.79 and 0.57 with FedProx), although it stays below pooled data (0.95 and 0.82). (3) In that case no lab gets a better model for its own substrates; what it gains is a model that also works on chemistry it has not yet tried. (4) Protecting single reactions with differential privacy (DP-SGD, ε ≈ 3–11 per lab) is affordable when labs hold different chemistry, but hiding a whole lab's participation is not possible with only five labs. Secure aggregation leaves accuracy unchanged and costs about 50 % more communication. Overall, without moving any data, federated learning recovered about 75–90 % of the gain in accuracy that pooling all data would give.

item.title: Spartan: Design and Recent Advances of a Molecular Modeling Program for Maximum Productivity in Research and Education
Influence of Magnetic Field Configuration on Vibrational Excitation and Ammonium Formation in Atmospheric-Pressure Plasma
item.description: Sustainable fertilizer production can benefit from approaches that can tune the relative production of nitrate and ammonium for different crop and soil requirements, as preferred NH4+/NO3- ratios vary among crops. In this work, the influence of external magnetic-field configuration on nitrogen product distribution in plasma-activated water was investigated using an atmospheric-pressure plasma reactor. Three permanent-magnet arrangements (linear, N/N pair, and jigsaw) were evaluated at N2 flow rates of 25 and 500 mL/min. At 25 mL/min, nitrate remained dominant across all conditions, with 93.9-98.7% mass selectivity. Conversely, at 500 mL/min, the magnetic configurations shifted the product distribution toward ammonium, increasing the NH4+/NO3- molar ratio from 0.25 without magnets to 1.20, 1.93, and 2.40 for the linear, N/N pair, and jigsaw configurations, respectively. Optical emission spectroscopy and vibrational-temperature analysis suggest that the magnetic field altered the plasma excitation environment, with higher ammonium selectivity at 500 mL/min associated with higher vibrational excitation. These results demonstrate that magnetic-field topology and gas flow rate can tune nitrogen-product selectivity in plasma activated water toward more targeted and sustainable fertilizer production.

item.title: Synthesis of Diversifiable Bicyclic Isoxazole Cores for Applications in Medicinal Chemistry and Drug Discovery
item.description: Partially saturated bicyclic scaffolds are valuable structural motifs in medicinal chemistry, combining C(sp3)-rich, three-dimensional structural features with spatially and electronically distinct (hetero)aromatic systems. Herein, we report an efficient synthetic approach to functionalized dihydroisoxazolopyridinones, providing access to an underexplored class of isoxazole-containing fused bicyclic scaffolds bearing synthetically versatile amine and ketone functionalities. The synthetic utility of these scaffolds was further demonstrated through complementary derivatization strategies, providing access to a structurally diverse range of derivatives and enabling systematic exploration of this chemical space.

item.title: Selective Lanthanide-Binding Peptides: Molecular Insights into Binding Affinity and Selectivity
item.description: Rare earth elements (REEs), including the lanthanides, are essential to clean-energy technologies, semiconductors, electric vehicles, turbines, and other advanced materials that exploit their luminescent, magnetic, and catalytic properties. Current REE separation methods, however, suffer from poor selectivity, high solvent use, and environmental burden, which motivates greener and more selective strategies. Here we combine fluorescence binding measurements, molecular dynamics, enhanced-sampling calculations, descriptor analysis, and machine learning to determine how lanthanide-binding tag (LBT) peptides discriminate among trivalent REE cations in aqueous solution. The peptides operate in two binding regimes. For larger, lighter REEs, affinity is governed primarily by ion size, solvation, solvent accessibility, and non-bonded electrostatic interactions in a loosely coordinated binding pocket. For smaller, heavier REEs, the pocket contracts, and steric crowding, ligand–ligand electrostatic repulsion, and backbone torsional strain increasingly oppose further stabilization. Correlation analyses with sequence-derived, solvation, ligation, and conformational descriptors support this dichotomy. Analysis of selected LBT1-derived variants yields design rules: terminal charge tunes absolute affinity, ligating-residue geometry controls productive electrostatic coordination, a gatekeeper residue regulates water access and steric closure, and terminal residue hydrophobicity modulates amphiphilicity while preserving lanthanide-size sensitivity. Finally, classifiers trained on 37,041 sequences predict coarse Tb3+ affinity classes from a few bioinformatic descriptors, including disorder propensity, charge, amphiphilicity, and hydrophobicity, whereas predicting relative affinity across the full lanthanide series remains sensitive to solvation and binding-pocket remodeling. These results provide a molecular framework for engineering peptides for selective REE recovery and separation.

item.title: Spatio-temporal air quality patterns and hotspot identification using a high-density, statewide sensor network in West Bengal, India
item.description: West Bengal, a state in India located in the lower Gangetic Plain, experiences severe air quality degradation from combined local and regional sources. Understanding spatiotemporal pollution dynamics across this densely populated state is crucial for designing effective air quality management strategies. We analyze four years of continuous monitoring data (2022–2026) from a statewide network of 314 sensor-based monitors deployed by the West Bengal Pollution Control Board, combined with reference-grade monitors, to characterize pollution patterns and identify actionable hotspots. Air quality management in India under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) has focused on reduction of PM10 levels in urban areas. Multi-pollutant Air Quality Index (AQI) analysis reveals a critical decoupling: while PM10 is the dominant pollutant at more than 80% of sites, PM2.5 drives the more severe pollution episodes (AQI >200), particularly in winter. Statewide annual average AQI remained Satisfactory between 2022 and 2025 and average winter AQI improved, declining from 112 to 99, yet annual average PM10 exceeded the national ambient air quality standard in every year. We developed a systematic hotspot classification framework that categorizes sites into operational classes, and identified 13 sites showing repeated off-season incidences of high AQI, indicative of local sources. Intra-city analysis in the six NCAP cities, which have the densest monitoring networks, allows us to identify locality-level variation and patterns. These findings demonstrate a need for airshed-based mitigation for most of the state, along with targeted interventions at identified hotspots.

item.title: LigandFF: an open-source implementation of rule-based atom typing, charge assignment and parameter assignment by analogy
item.description: The CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF) covers drug-like molecules through an automated assignment program that types atoms, assigns charges from bond-charge increments, and transfers missing bonded parameters from analogous ones with an associated penalty. The algorithms are published, but the program and its two hand-built rule files are distributed only in binary form. We describe LigandFF, an open-source reimplementation built exclusively from the published algorithms and the public CGenFF 5.0 topology, parameter and charge-increment files. LigandFF implements the published ring, resonance and aromaticity perception, the rule language for atom typing, the bond-charge-increment scheme with peratom charge penalties, the penalty-weighted analogy search, halogen lone pairs, and writes CHARMM stream files, PSF files and OpenMM and GROMACS inputs. Its typing rules were written against the CGenFF training molecules, and its substitution-penalty matrices were fitted to 5,787 analogies that the official program recorded in the parameter file. On held-out test splits, LigandFF types 97.4% and 97.8% of two sets of CGenFF training molecules with every atom correct (99.7% and 99.6% of atoms). Replaying the analogies recorded in the parameter file against the database they were made from, it recovers the official program’s choice of source parameter for 92.1% of 1,447 held-out cases. It reproduces the program-5.0 charges and penalties printed in the CGenFF 5.0 supporting information exactly, and all 2,074 benchmark molecules produce systems that build in OpenMM. All references are CGenFF training molecules or outputs of the official program that are already public; agreement with the official program on new drug-like molecules has not been measured. LigandFF is not the official CGenFF program, and its outputs are labelled accordingly.

item.title: Dual-Target Structural Discovery of Orally Bioavailable Selective KRAS G12D Inhibitors Accelerated by Deterministic Sub-100 μs Userspace PCIe BAR0 MMIO Spatial Voxel Screening
Accuracy and Limits of Pretrained Interatomic Potentials Across Molecular Reaction Pathways
item.description: Foundation models of machine-learning interatomic potentials are now used to search for reaction pathways, but the common reactive test sets share structures with the training data for several of these models. We compare energies and forces from fifteen pretrained models with DFT single-point values at fixed GFN2-xTB-derived geometries from 9,017 gas-phase reaction pathways in DORTS-9K, a separately generated dataset, and extend the comparison to seventeen models for the reactions that contain only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen (CHNO). Models trained on molecular data are the most accurate, and the best of them, UMA-M OMol, has a median force RMSE of 0.018 eV Å⁻¹ and reproduces 96% of the 3,713 CHNO barriers within 1 kcal mol⁻¹. Force errors increase from the endpoints to the transition-state anchors for all molecular models, nearly doubling for UMA-M OMol. Across the 38 CHNO reactions with the largest UMA-M OMol barrier errors, all models except AIMNet2 and AIMNet2-RXN underestimate the DFT barriers by 6.5–85.2% across models and reactions. These include hydrogen transfers involving nitrous acid and an azide/isocyanate template.

item.title: Photochemical Activation of Glycyl Radical Enzymes Bypasses Radical SAM Activating Enzymes
item.description: Glycyl radical enzymes (GREs) catalyze diverse radical transformations with considerable potential for biocatalysis; however, their functional characterization and synthetic application have been limited by their dependence on partner radical S-adenosylmethionine (rSAM) activating enzymes (AEs), which are often challenging to express and purify. Herein, we report a nonenzymatic strategy for initiating GRE catalysis through short-wavelength UV irradiation, bypassing the need for rSAM AEs. Using benzylsuccinate synthase (BSS), we achieved stereoselective C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation in up to 92 ± 8% assay yield. This approach was extended to two additional GRE hydroalkylases, including 2methylnaphthylsuccinate synthase (NMSS), whose conventional in vitro activation had remained inaccessible. Furthermore, photochemical activation enabled product formation by glycerol dehydratase (GDH) and indoleacetate decarboxylase (IAD), demonstrating applicability across three distinct GRE classes. Wavelength-dependence and mechanistic experiments support photochemical initiation of the native GRE catalytic cycle, with catalysis continuing after irradiation is stopped. These findings establish a general proof-of-principle strategy for accessing GREcatalyzed transformations photochemically and provide a foundation for developing more selective and efficient photochemical activation methods.

item.title: Parallel and Resource-Efficient Bayesian Reaction Optimization
item.description: Reaction optimization, central to both synthetic method development and process chemistry, has been accelerated by two largely independent strategies: Bayesian optimization (BO) uses a probabilistic surrogate model to select the most informa-tive experiments, while high-throughput experimentation (HTE) evaluates many conditions in parallel. In practice, HTE plates are typically designed as combinatorial grids, so that one stock solution can be dispensed across a full row or column in a single operation. Batched BO, by contrast, selects each well independently and disregards this structure, producing plates that are laborious to prepare without specialized dispensing equipment. Here we introduce PlateOpt, a BO framework that designs entire well plates rather than individual reactions, proposing optimized grids, such as eight ligands crossed with three bases and two solvents, that can be readily executed with multichannel pipettes or simple liquid handlers. On two retrospective HTE benchmarks, constraining batches to PlateOpt layouts led to only minor loss in optimization performance. PlateOpt came within 6–9 percentage points of unconstrained batch BO while reducing preparative effort by up to ten-fold. Applied prospectively to the copper-catalyzed etherification of 4-bromoanisole with hexan-1-ol, PlateOpt raised the yield from 14.5% to 72.0% within six 48-condition plates, exploring 1.0% of a 28,800-condition search space. The optimized conditions afforded 99% yield in batch. Mechanistic investigations indicate that a Cu(II) bis(oxalamide) catalyst is active under conditions previously connected to a Cu(I) cycle. By designing plates that are both informative and practical to execute, PlateOpt makes data-efficient, closed-loop optimization accessible to any laboratory performing parallel experimentation.

item.title: Emergence of Atomic Energy States of One-Electron Systems by Single Equation: Nucleus-Driven Causal Information Propagation in Real Space
item.description: Although probabilistic electron wave-function approaches provide solid mechanistic insights for atoms and molecules, their inherent reliance on static, boundary-dependent approximations limits the direct description of real space. This study demonstrates the emergence of highly accurate atomic energy states by a single nucleus-driven causal information-propagating framework without boundary conditions. When compared with NIST ionization energy data for one-electron systems, this model generates a less than 0.01% relative error for the hydrogen-like atom (Z = 1 ~ 67) and less than 0.25% up to Ra (Z=88), where the energy spectrum naturally emerges from the nucleus as wave maximum peaks in real space by relying solely on the atomic number (Z) as an independent variable alongside fixed global parameters. These highly accurate predictions emerge through the tracking of the irreversible and continuous propagation of causal information. Comparisons with the emergent Lagrangian path confirmed that macroscopic trajectories and wave behaviors autonomously emerge from the collective accumulation of local information events. Ultimately, these results successfully shows the macroscopic pattern generation of ionization energies of one-electron system can be emerged by the propagation of causal information of the nucleus in real space and its macroscopic energy trends are governed by a single rule.

item.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
item.description: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

item.title: Hierarchical formulation optimization for accelerated discovery of chemical mixtures
item.description: The design of chemical mixtures, or formulations, is a critical yet challenging aspect of materials science due to the combinatorial explosion of possible ingredient and composition variations. Traditional trial-and-error methods are costly, especially when optimizing for multiple target properties concurrently. To accelerate formulation discovery, we developed a multiparameter, hierarchical optimization framework that integrates high-throughput machine learning (ML) predictions with sophisticated search algorithms. The optimization workflow is data-source agnostic, functioning with both experimental and simulated inputs. We first benchmarked optimization algorithms using a large, self-consistent dataset of simulated solvent mixtures to isolate algorithmic search efficiency from experimental noise. We then rigorously benchmarked various optimization algorithms. For composition optimization, the differential evolution algorithm was identified as the most robust and efficient method, rapidly identifying optimal compositions with minimal ML prediction calls. For ingredient selection, a genetic algorithm (GA) significantly outperformed brute force, random, and Bayesian optimization approaches, finding a much higher proportion of top-performing formulations with the fewest samples. By coupling GA for ingredient selection with differential evolution for composition refinement, the hierarchical workflow successfully maximized a multiparameter optimization score across diverse materials applications, including minimizing solvent viscosity, maximizing drug solubility, and maximizing motor octane number. Representative optimized formulation candidates were subsequently evaluated using classical molecular dynamics simulations to independently validate the property trends predicted by the data-driven optimization approach. This work highlights a robust, intelligent, and rapid computer-aided workflow for navigating the complex design space of chemical mixtures, minimizing the need for extensive physical experimentation and accelerating the discovery of high-performing, tailored formulations.

item.title: Five-Year Doubling of Groundwater Trifluoroacetic Acid Concentrations and Associations with Agricultural Indicators
item.description: Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is an extremely persistent and highly mobile substance accumulating in the environment due to increasing emissions of TFA and its precursors from diverse sources, with rising concentrations also documented in food and humans. Yet direct evidence of recent increases in groundwater remains scarce, despite growing concern. We analyzed official Austrian monitoring data from 2018–2019 and 2024, including 16 sites sampled in both periods. TFA concentrations increased at all 16 sites; mean concentrations rose from 1.36 to 2.86 μg/L (+110%) and median concentrations from 1.01 to 2.05 μg/L (+103%). Across all sites, mean concentrations were 0.78 and 2.42 μg/L and median concentrations were 0.39 and 1.40 μg/L, respectively. The comparison is consistent with a broader upward shift but cannot establish a national temporal rate of TFA accumulation. To assess agriculture as a possible source, we tested associations with agricultural contamination indicators. TFA was associated with nitrate and pesticide burden, even after spatial adjustment, but not with the sum of 27 other monitored PFAS. Together with European source evidence, these associations support a substantial agricultural contribution. Given TFA's persistence and limited removal by conventional water treatment, reducing emissions from TFA-forming pesticides and other sources, such as fluorinated gases, is critical to limit further long-term accumulation toward or beyond levels of concern.

item.title: Protactinium, Neptunium, and Plutonium Solubilization and Extraction Mediated by Polyoxometalates
item.description: Understanding how chelators impact solubility, complexation, and partitioning of early actinides is essential for nuclear applications. Herein, we investigate how the aqueous speciation of protactinium, neptunium, and plutonium is impacted by three main polyoxometalates (POMs) topologies as inorganic chelators: the Wells-Dawson α2-P2W17O6110- (P2W17), the Keggin-type POMs PW11O397- (PW11), SiW11O398- (SiW11), GeW11O398- (GeW11), and BW11O399- (BW11), and a Lindqvist-type POM W5O186- (W5). These six POMs stabilize Pu(IV) in water, exemplified by crystallization of a new Pu-POM compound, Cs12PuIV(SiW11O39)2·H2O. Additionally, P2W17, PW11, SiW11 and GeW11 trigger reduction of the usually stable neptunyl(V) ion, [NpO2]+, and form [NpIV(POM)2]n- complexes, which is effective at both millimolar and tracer-level concentrations. In contrast, W5 and BW11 do not promote [NpO2]+ reduction under the tested conditions. Negatively-charged POM complexes render Np(IV) and Pu(IV) extractible via liquid-liquid extraction with quaternary ammonium Aliquat® 336 in kerosene. While protactinium typically requires highly corrosive fluoride solutions to solubilize, the POMs complex and solubilize it under mild conditions (pH ~5 and without fluoride), unlocking Pa extraction with quaternary ammonium. Quantitative separation of 233Pa/237Np is achieved with the combination of POMs plus Aliquat® 336, yielding >99% radiopurity 233Pa and 237Np in a single step (separation factor Pa/Np > 1300). Experiments with the long-lived 231Pa also revealed that POMs increase the solubility of Pa2O5·nH2O(s), overcoming both Pa(V) hydrolysis and competitive complexation with fluoride. This study unravels a general strategy for POM-mediated reduction of neptunyl(V) to Np(IV) in water and separation of Pa, Np, and Pu. This is the first reported complexation of protactinium with POMs, expanding the chemical toolkit to study this elusive element.

item.title: Hydrophobic Interaction as the Resolution of Interfacial Frustration
item.description: The hydrophobic effect is a solvent-mediated phenomenon in aqueous molecular systems, with consequences for liquid interfaces, self-assembly, polymer collapse and protein organisation. Contemporary statistical-mechanical frameworks explain much of its thermodynamics, including the dependence of hydration on solute size, density fluctuations and interfacial formation. The remaining conceptual challenge is not the absence of successful theories, but the lack of a common spatial language for describing how heterogeneous non-polar interfaces perturb the collective state of water. In this paper, I propose interfacial frustration as such a descriptor: a spatially distributed representation of the mismatch between the statistically preferred state of interfacial water and the geometric constraints imposed by a non-polar interface. Hydrophobic association is considered as a solvent-mediated reorganisation and, in appropriate cases, a reduction or redistribution of this mismatch, while retaining the established thermodynamic description in terms of free energy (G), enthalpy (H), entropy (S) and density fluctuations. The framework is intended as a complementary representation, not a replacement for existing theories such as Lum-Chandler-Weeks (LCW) theory. A component-resolved operational representation is specified, and its potential application to water–n-alkane interfaces and aqueous polymer collapse is developed as a proposed analytical programme. A more tentative extension to protein dynamics is also retained. These applications are proposed tests, not empirical validation of the framework. Its value depends on whether the spatial pattern and non-additivity of interfacial frustration provide predictive information beyond established surface-area, density, intermolecular-interaction and conformational-ensemble descriptors

item.title: Plasma-Enhanced Surface Doping of SnNiOx Nanofilms for Water Oxidation
item.description: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) limits the efficiency of alkaline water electrolysis, and the rational design of non-precious-metal anodes requires an understanding of how a dopant modifies an oxide surface. Although atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer high intrinsic activity, precise synthesis and characterization of their local active sites remain challenging. Surface doping provides a tractable alternative for probing intrinsic activity and correlating it with the dopant coordination environment. Here we use plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PE-ALD) to deposit sub-monolayer doses of Fe and Co on ultrathin SnNiOx films grown on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO). We vary the Fe and Co dopant coordination environment using oxidizing (O2) or reducing (H2) plasma as an independent variable on the dopant deposition step. item.title: A Gaussian-mixture approximation for Marcus kinetics of electron transfer at metal electrodes
item.description: We develop a Gaussian-mixture approximation for electron transfer (GM-ET) at metal electrodes, which accurately approximates the rate integral in Marcus-Hush-Chidsey (MHC) and electron-coupled ion-transfer (ECIT) kinetics. We adapt the normal-mixture formulas of Monahan and Stefanski (1989) to approximate the Gaussian–logistic convolution for the Marcus ET rate integrated over the Fermi-Dirac statistics of electron energies, under the wide-band approximation and with equal reorganization energies for reduction and oxidation. A calibrated two-component mixture approximates the sum of reduction and oxidation rate constants, from which the individual rate constants are reconstructed using their exact thermodynamic ratio to preserve detailed balance. Compared with the widely used asymptotic matching formula of Zeng et al. (2014), GM-ET reduces the largest sampled relative rate error from 35 % to 0.13 % over the evaluated domain. Fits to current–overpotential curves calculated from the full integral show that GM-ET also improves the recovery of reorganization energy and limiting rate constant, reducing errors associated with compensation between these parameters. GM-ET’s greater accuracy at the formal potential further reduces errors in the standard rate constant calculated from the fitted parameters. GM-ET thus provides an explicit current expression and analytical derivatives with improved accuracy for kinetic calculations and parameter estimation.

item.title: Structure-Function Relationships for Cobalt-Quinol Electrocatalysts for Dioxygen Reduction and Comparison with Iron-Quinol Analogues
item.description: We report Co(II) and Co(III) complexes with three polydentate quinol-containing ligands: N,N’-bis(2,5-dihydroxybenzyl)-N,N’-bis(2-pyridinylmethyl)-1,2-ethylenediamine (H4qp2), N-(2,5-dihydroxybenzyl)-N,N’-bis(2-pyridinylmethyl)-1,2-ethylenediamine (H2qp3), and 1,8bis(2,5-dihydroxybenzyl)-1,4,8,11-tetraazacyclotetradecane (H4qp4). The cobalt compounds with H4qp2 and H2qp3 electrocatalytically reduce O2 to H2O2 and H2O in acetate buffered acetonitrile (MeCN). With H2qp3, O2 is reduced to an approximately equimolar mixture of H2O and H2O2; whereas, the Co(II)-H4qp2 complex preferentially produces H2O, albeit with a higher overpotential. A similar enhancement in water selectivity between H2qp3 and H4qp2 was previously observed by our groups for Fe(II) complexes. Comparative studies of the new catalysts reported here with previously reported cobalt and iron catalysts with polydentate quinol-containing ligands reveal that the intermolecular acid-dependent rate constants (kH) measured for each complex strongly correlate with product distribution, with larger kH yielding greater water selectivity. We propose that this correlation is related to a common M(III)-OOH intermediate in the catalytic cycle where the rapid contribution of additional electron-proton equivalents from the catalysts drives the production of H2O over H2O2. The measured pKa values of the catalysts are consistent with them existing as metal-bound quinolates in acetate buffered MeCN. The redoxactive ligands therefore primarily contribute electrons during the product-determining step with the acetic acid from the buffer providing protons.

item.title: A hydrophilic Fe(III) macrocyclic T1 MRI probe with an iron grip and enhanced relaxivity through base-catalyzed proton exchange
item.description: Two high-spin Fe(III) complexes containing a bis(phenolato)-1,4,7-triazacyclononane framework and either an ancillary sulfonate pendant (Fe-CREST) or a benzyl substituent (Fe-BEAT) were prepared as members of a new macrocyclic ligand framework for high-spin Fe(III) T1 MRI probes. Fe-BEAT was not soluble in water above 0.5 mM while the sulfonated macrocyclic complex Fe-CREST was soluble to at least 100 mM, one of the most water-soluble Fe(III) probes reported to date. Both complexes exhibited apparent ionization of inner-sphere water with 𝑝𝐾𝑎 values near 7.2. Fe-CREST demonstrated base-catalyzed proton exchange relaxation enhancement attributed to water ligand protons. Despite having an available coordination site for binding water or other ligands, Fe-CREST resisted bicarbonate, phosphate, ascorbate, and apo-transferrin challenge and showed no detectable transfer of iron to a 10fold excess of the high-affinity chelator HBED (N,N′-bis(2-hydroxybenzyl)ethylenediamine-N,N′diacetic acid) over 7 days at 37 °C. The complex retains strong longitudinal MRI relaxivity (𝒓𝟏 = 2.1 mM−1 s−1, 7 T, 37 ºC), and its hydrophilic character produces a biodistribution profile characteristic of an extracellular agent with rapid, predominantly renal elimination in mice, supported by detection of Fe-CREST by mass spectrometry analysis of urine. At a matched dose, Fe-CREST produced greater liver and gallbladder enhancement than gadoterate meglumine (DOTAREM), consistent with a secondary hepatobiliary route.

item.title: Predicted modulation of TATB-polymer adhesion by methacrylate side-chain chemistry
item.description: Many high explosive formulations are composites that combine organic energetic molecular crystals with a small quantity of polymer as a binder to impart mechanical strength. Crystal-polymer adhesion plays an important role in determining composite strength, but clear structure-property relationships that link the underlying chemistries of the energetic crystal and broad polymer-binder design space remain poorly understood. To this end, we apply a classical molecular dynamics (MD) modeling framework to predict the molecular-scale energetic contribution to crystal-polymer adhesion between the crystalline explosive TATB (1,3,5-triamino-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene) and functionalized methacrylate polymers within an oligomer approximation. The polymer series maintains a consistent backbone, but modulates the side-chain chemistry to assess the roles of steric hindrance, fluorination, hydrogen bonding, and aromaticity in promoting strong interactions with TATB, an aromatic molecular crystal that forms two-dimensional hydrogen-bonded layers. All oligomers considered exhibit energetically favorable adhesion with the two lowest-energy TATB crystal facets, and with negligible facet anisotropy for a given chemistry, despite the 50% difference in the two TATB surface energies. The predicted adhesion-energy ranking by side-chain chemistry is hydroxyethyl > phenyl > alkyl > pentafluoroethyl, with adhesion energies differing by up to 30% across this set. Interfacial structure, site-specific surface interaction characteristics, and oligomer binding energy were assessed, showing that side-chain chemistry can strongly influence adhesive contacts in ways that directly trace to the local nanometer-scale environment of the crystal-polymer interface. These results show that selective modification of side-chain chemistry can promote strong polymer contacts with molecular crystals having strongly anisotropic surface energies and provide a computational benchmark with testable chemical hypotheses amenable to future experimental validation.

item.title: Synthetic Validation of Nucleophilic O–O Coupling with a Terminal Co-Oxo Complex
item.description: *Corresponding author email: jsanderson@uchicago.edu Abstract In nature, O2 is produced via water oxidation at the oxygen-evolving complex within the photosystem II protein complex found in plants.1 Deeper mechanistic understanding of O–O bond formation, the key step in oxygen evolution, would greatly inform renewable energy technologies based on water splitting. Studies on oxygen evolution have led to two primary mechanisms for OO bond formation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide or water on a high-valent metal-oxo intermediate or radical coupling of two metal-oxo moieties.2 Due to the fleeting nature of the key intermediates in water oxidation, there is no conclusive evidence favoring one mechanism over another. However, recent theoretical studies hint at a third mechanistic paradigm: nucleophilic OO coupling.3,4 Here we report the reaction of a nucleophilic Co(III)-oxo complex with electrophilic O-atom transfer reagents that results in O–O bond formation. Experimental and computational analyses support that O-atom transfer occurs via a nucleophilic O–O coupling mechanism, experimentally validating the viability of nucleophilic O–O coupling involving a metal–oxo. These results provide experimental support for a similar mechanism of O–O bond formation between a nucleophilic Mn-oxo and an electrophilic, bridging Mn-oxo in the oxygen evolving complex.

item.title: Supramolecular Viscoelastic Systems for Next-Generation Electronic Packaging and Soft Electronics: Assembly, Rheology, Electro-Thermal Transport, and PFAS- and Microplastic-Free Sustainability
item.description: Modern electronic packaging and soft electronic architectures face a converging engineering and environmental imperative: sustaining reliable dielectric insulation, capacitive coupling, mechanical compliance, and high-flux thermal dissipation under escalating power densities, while phasing out environmentally persistent per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and non-reworkable crosslinked polymers that generate secondary microplastics across the electronic waste lifecycle. Supramolecular viscoelastic systems—constructed from reversible non-covalent interactions including directional hydrogen bonding, electrostatic coacervation, host–guest inclusion, amphiphilic self-assembly, and dynamic ionic or metal–ligand coordination—offer an intelligent, adaptive materials platform capable of bridging this gap. By decoupling processing rheology from in-service structural stability, these stimuli-responsive networks span a continuous spectrum from shear-thinning viscoelastic fluids and bicontinuous mesophases to clay-like, strain-stiffening yield-stress solids. This review synthesizes recent advances (predominantly 2024–2026) across the structure–property–sustainability continuum of supramolecular viscoelastic systems for electronics. We examine molecular design rules and mesoscale assembly pathways, linear and nonlinear rheological dynamics under multi-stimuli actuation, broadband dielectric dispersion and capacitive gap filling, phonon-mediated thermal transport and adaptive thermal interface materials (TIMs), and circularity strategies for PFAS and microplastics elimination under Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design (SSbD) frameworks. Key reliability bottlenecks—including moisture stability, DC breakdown strength, high-temperature creep resistance, and scalable solvent-free processing—are delineated to guide industrial qualification.

item.title: Recent Advances in Glass-Based Printed Circuit Board Technologies: Silicate Network Chemistry, Ceramic-Reinforced Composites, Interfacial Engineering, and the Post-PFAS Transition
item.description: Purpose – This review evaluates recent (2024–2026) advances in glass-based and ceramic-reinforced glass printed circuit board (PCB) substrates as chemically inert, halogen-free alternatives to polymeric laminates facing dielectric, thermomechanical, and regulatory constraints. Design/methodology/approach – A chemistry- and ceramics-focused synthesis of 157 post-2023 peerreviewed studies integrates silicate network chemistry, glass-ceramic crystallization, broadband dielectric relaxation, high-field breakdown physics, fracture toughening, through-glass via (TGV) metallurgy, and post-PFAS lifecycle analyses. Findings – Alkali-free aluminoborosilicate networks and ceramic-reinforced glass-ceramics achieve silicon-matched thermal expansion (3.1–3.8 ppm·K-1), low gigahertz dissipation (tan δ < 0.003), elevated thermal stability (>650 °C), and zero per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) or thermoset microplastic emissions. Phase-controlled reinforcements, cristobalite suppression, fluorine-free silanol passivation, and laser-induced TGV processing overcome intrinsic glass brittleness and interfacial copper adhesion barriers. Practical implications – The synthesis provides actionable formulation, sintering, and metallization guidelines for AI/HPC chiplet packaging, 5G/6G millimeter-wave interconnects, and wide-bandgap power modules, framed within a 2024–2035 scale-up roadmap. Originality/value – Unlike process-centric interposer surveys, this review unifies atomic-scale glass chemistry, ceramic phase engineering, interfacial reliability, and cross-sectoral post-PFAS circularity into a coherent framework for next-generation sustainable microelectronic packaging.

item.title: Using Graphene Oxide Coatings to Filter Microplastics Out of Water
item.description: Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 millimeters. They include long fibers from textiles, irregular fragments, and thin films. They are now found in rivers, lakes, and drinking water, and this is becoming a serious problem. Ordinary filter paper has pores that are too large to stop most of these particles, so they pass through. This project tested whether a thin coating of graphene oxide (GO) could turn ordinary paper into a better barrier. We made GO from graphite powder by chemical oxidation and placed it on standard cellulose filter paper to make an affordable filter. In a first trial, the plain paper filter caught only about 11.2% of the microplastic in the water, while the GO-coated filter caught about 94.0%. The GO filter was also much slower: 1.08 mL/min compared with 5.88 to 8.50 mL/min for plain paper. This pattern is consistent with a physical barrier effect, in which the GO layer holds particles back at the paper surface and also slows the water. The first trial used one run per condition and different sample volumes (50 mL and 20 mL), so it is only preliminary. The study was therefore repeated with equal inputs, triplicate runs, and two extra controls, yielding a salt-corrected retention efficiency of 91.4 ± 1.8% for the GO-coated membrane compared with 10.5 ± 1.2% for plain filter paper (mean ± SD, n = 3). Overall, the results suggest that a simple, low-cost GO coating may improve microplastic removal, and that the idea is worth testing further to protect local waterways.

item.title: Extending Data-Dense Transient Methods to Back-mixed Flow Reactors using DIRT – Deconvolution Informed by Residence Time distributions
item.description: Transient flow as a kinetic data collection technique has so far relied on the plug-flow assumption. We introduce DIRT (Deconvolution Informed by Residence Time distributions) to extend it to back-mixed systems, demonstrated on a solid-forming Aldol condensation. DIRT-corrected concentration and residence time ramps match independent steadystate measurements and yield a kinetic model, obtained with ~80% less experiment time and solvent than steady-state methods.

item.title: Molecular Assembly Enumeration vs. 1D Dictionary Compression Across the Nano-DrugBank Small-Molecule Repository
item.description: Assembly Theory (AT) defines the Molecular Assembly Index (MA) as the minimal number of recursive bonddisjoint subgraph-joining steps required to construct a 2D molecular graph [1, 2, 4], whereas critics from Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) contend that empirical MA rankings collapse to standard 1D dictionary compression applied to molecular strings [5, 6, 15]. Here, we evaluate MA against wrapped zlib (RFC 1950), headerless raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951), and header-free 256-ASCII Welch LZW across the Chodera Lab Nano-DrugBank small-molecule repository (N = 5,653, curated from DrugBank 4.5.0) [20–24] using the C++ branchand-bound solver (assemblycpp-v5) [4] under operating-system process isolation on an Apple M3 Ultra workstation. Applying RDKit valence sanitization, parent-fragment desalting (60 salts), stereochemistry-stripped Kekulé MDL V2000 serialization, and a 600 s per-subprocess wall-clock timeout yielded 5,520 resolved records (97.65%; MA in [1, 36], median MA = 14, median subprocess wall time 15.42 ms, mean 3,051 ms; conditional on the inspected two-argument repository runner pending a hash-logged rerun), 35 RDKit valence rejections (0.62%), and 98 computationally unresolved valid graphs (1.73%): 87 with subprocess runtime right-censored at 600 s (median Nheavy = 77) and 11 macrocycles/polypeptides (median Nheavy = 128) explicitly logging the solver's internal Subgraph enumeration limit reached (ENUM_MAX = 50,000,000) diagnostic between 375.8 and 578.2 s. Among resolved records (median Nheavy = 23), 2,429 (44.00%) satisfy MA ≥ 15 [1, 2]. Per-character compression ratios span more than twofold ranges within fixed-MA slices, and in in-sample linear ordinary least-squares (OLS) models adjusting for heavy-atom count (Nheavy), compressed lengths explain 38.6% (DEFLATE: partial r = +0.6212) and 32.0% (Welch LZW: partial r = +0.5656) of Nheavy-adjusted MA variance on stereochemistrystripped canonical parent SMILES (38.4% and 31.7% across n = 5,274 unique parent strings; 42.9% and 38.8% on Kekulé charge/isotope-stripped V2000 graph SMILES, or 42.3% and 38.1% across n = 5,254 unique keys). Across all tested specifications, 57.1%–68.3% of in-sample Nheavy-adjusted linear MA variance remains unexplained, showing that the evaluated 1D SMILES compressors and 2D MA are positively correlated yet not linearly interchangeable.

item.title: Secondary Organic Aerosol Formation from Cleaning Product Use in a Residential Kitchen
item.description: Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) can form indoors when volatile organic compounds (VOCs), commonly emitted from the use of scented cleaning products and other chemical products, undergo oxidation and condense onto aerosols. Indoor oxidants can come from a variety of sources, including the use of chlorine bleach for surface cleaning and disinfection, operation of germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) lamps for air disinfection, and penetration of ozone (O3) from the outdoor environment. During the Consumer products, Lights, and Environmental Air cleaning in Normal conditions (CLEAN) Home Study, we measured SOA formation in a real home after performing surface cleaning with a scented all-purpose cleaning liquid and subsequently introducing different indoor oxidant scenarios. Six oxidant scenarios were tested, including (1) bleach surface cleaning, (2) O3 injection, (3) 222 nm GUV (GUV222) lamp operation, (4) 254 nm GUV (GUV254) lamp operation, and bleach surface cleaning with subsequent (5) GUV222 or (6) GUV254 lamp operation. Spraying the cleaning liquid emitted high concentrations of large primary particles and monoterpenes indoors. SOA formation occurred after cleaning liquid application and subsequent oxidant introduction for all oxidant scenarios except for bleach cleaning without subsequent GUV illumination. The oxidant scenario that led to the most SOA formation was bleach cleaning with GUV254 lamp operation. We used a chemical kinetic model to simulate monoterpene and aerosol concentrations indoors during cleaning liquid experiments with three oxidant scenarios: O3 injection, GUV222 lamp operation, and GUV254 lamp operation. We compared model results to our measurements for these select experiments. Results from this study demonstrate that indoor cleaning activities can lead to significant SOA formation in real indoor environments.

item.title: Transducing a CO2 Concentration Gradient into Electrical Energy through Copper–Ethylenediamine Coordination
item.description: A gas-phase concentration gradient contains Gibbs free energy, while converting this energy into electricity requires a chemical transduction mechanism. Here, we convert a CO2 concentration gradient into a Cu redox-potential difference through copper–ethylenediamine coordination. Ethylenediamine (eda) acts as a bifunctional molecular transducer: its coordination stabilizes the Cu2+ state, whereas CO2-induced protonation of eda diminishes coordination ability and stabilizes the metallic Cu. A cell consisting of copper electrodes and copper–ethylenediamine electrolyte generates an open-circuit voltage of 120 mV under a CO2/N2 gradient. A peak power density of 26.3 mW m−2 was achieved with a dialysis membrane, and Faradaic current was sustained for approximately 48 h. pH-dependent redox potentials and CO2 concentration-dependent pH shifts account for the generated open-circuit voltage. These results demonstrate a molecular strategy for coupling the chemical-potential difference associated with a CO2 concentration gradient to electrical output through linked acid–base, coordination, and redox equilibria without direct CO2 reduction.

item.title: Rh(III)-Catalyzed Regiodivergent Enantioselective C2- and C4–H Alkylation of Indoles
item.description: Switchable regiodivergent asymmetric synthesis constitutes a powerful paradigm in asymmetric catalysis, which greatly expands synthetic versatility and allows the efficient assembly of structurally diverse chiral molecules. Herein, we report a switchable regiodivergent enantioselective C–H functionalization of indoles with nitroalkenes, delivering a tunable platform to access C2- and C4-functionalized chiral indole derivatives with high efficiency, as well as excellent regio- and enantioselectivity (up to 97% yield, 96% ee, and >10:1 rr). Simply tuning the reaction parameters enables divergent C–H activation and enantioselective functionalization of electronically similar C(sp2)–H bonds within indole frameworks. Combined experimental and computational studies elucidate the mechanistic origins governing this remarkable regio- and enantioselectivity.

item.title: Selectivity for Fe versus Carbonyl Centered Silylation in Low-Valent β-Diketiminate Fe Complexes
item.description: Understanding the changes in reactivity and selectivity engendered by weak-field supporting ligands and multimetallic complexes offers new opportunities in organometallic chemistry. Here, we examine the selectivity of reactions of silyl electrophiles with monometallic iron-carbonyl complexes, which can lead to silylation either at the metal to form a silyl complex, or at a CO ligand to give a carbyne complex. The first mode of reactivity is common with classic organometallic complexes, and the latter has been observed more recently with complexes with strong-field ligands. More recently, bridging CO complexes with weak-field β-diketiminate ligands have been observed to give carbyne products as well, implying that the bridging CO ligands are nucleophilic in this environment. However, it was not clear whether the key determinant of CO reactivity was the ligand field strength or the bridging of the CO ligand. Here, these influences are decoupled by studying silylation of monomeric iron(0) dicarbonyl and tricarbonyl complexes with the same weak-field β-diketiminate ligand. We show that silylation at the iron, at the CO, or at THF can dominate. A particularly interesting product comes from THF silylation, followed by nucleophilic attack by Fe to give ring-opening and very rapid migration of a transient iron-alkyl complex to CO. DFT studies confirm that the β-diketiminate supported complexes undergo much more rapid alkyl migration than the analogous reaction in classic cyclopentadienyliron complexes.
