Suitable for large-scale studies, with a runtime of 25 min per sample that includes robotic sample preparation and data acquisition, this work describes an analytical framework to ensure high data quality in human biomonitoring and exposomics studies. It requires a low volume of biospecimen, 0.1 mL of plasma, and maintains compatibility with parallel LC-MS workflows for enhancing chemical space coverage. A rigorous quality control strategy was implemented, using the apparent recovery as a key parameter for evaluating performance in GC-HRMS. Isooctane was selected as the extraction solvent for yielding the highest overall apparent recoveries for a targeted panel of 106 persistent organic pollutants (PCBs, PBDEs, PCDDs, OCPs) and PAHs. The final workflow includes >180 anthropogenic compounds for which authentic reference standards potentially enable Level 1 identifications. Three approaches for sensitivity assessment were discussed, resulting in limits of quantification ranging from 0.2 to 2.0 ng/mL. Procedural calibration, with fortified biological samples and cohort-specific pooled QC samples, is proposed to effectively correct for matrix interferences and ensure accurate (semi-)quantification across analytical batches. The final analytical design confirmed the fitness-for-purpose of the automated-LLE-GC-HRMS pipeline. The integration of NIST SRM 1958 served as a benchmark for in-house long-term stability and inter-lab comparability. The potential of retrospective data analysis for emerging contaminants is demonstrated by non-targeted analysis (NTA) of commercially available pooled plasma and the two certified reference material SRM1950, and SRM1958. This scalable, standardized framework addresses limitations in sample availability while providing the reliability needed for exposome-wide association studies (ExWAS).

item.title: ExFiT: Ensemble-based Excited-State Character Fingerprinting across Temperatures
item.description: The character of electronically excited states, such as the balance between local excitation (LE), charge transfer (CT), and the spatial separation of electron and hole densities, strongly influences absorption properties and the electronic-state landscape at the Franck–Condon geometry of organic chromophores, evaluated at ground-state nuclear configurations. Conventional analyses based on single equilibrium geometries neglect thermal fluctuations that can significantly alter this character. We present ExFiT, an ensemble-based computational pipeline that interfaces with GPU-accelerated electronic-structure calculations for fingerprinting excited-state character across temperatures. ExFiT combines finite-temperature Wigner sampling with ensemble-resolved excited-state analysis and principal component analysis to quantify distributions of CT metrics, electron-hole separation, entanglement, and orbital participation. Application to representative chromophores (trans-azobenzene, (E)-hemithioindigo, para-nitroaniline, and coumarin 481) reveals distinct regimes of thermal behavior, ranging from robust excited-state character to broadened descriptor distributions and bright-state reordering associated with closely spaced excited states within the Franck–Condon ensemble. NTO overlap further shows that changes in optical brightness need not reflect changes in excited-state character, distinguishing state perturbation from state reassignment. These results demonstrate how thermal fluctuations modulate excited-state electronic structures and establish the applicability of ExFiT as a framework for generating statistically meaningful initial-condition ensembles for spectral simulations and future nonadiabatic dynamics studies.

item.title: Programmable Nanofluidic Confinement: From Static Nanotopographies to Reversible Electrokinetic Trapping
item.description: Single-molecule analysis increasingly relies on the ability to immobilize, confine, and manipulate biomolecules in solution. Nanofluidic devices provide a powerful route to this goal by using embedded nanotopographies on-chip to define free-energy landscapes that enable spatial manipulation, transport, confinement, and conformations that can be leveraged for biomedical applications. One classic example for molecular confinement is DNA extension in nanochannels, which has allowed for high-throughput genomic sequencing on-chip. Classic nanofluidic devices however are often limited by the static nature of their confinement landscapes, which are fixed by the static geometry of the device after fabrication, not allowing for real-time manipulation. Examples from optics (e.g. optical tweezers, optical lattices, holographic optical tweezers) demonstrate that, in principle, it is possible to achieve high-throughput dynamic control by using external fields to impose and alter confinement. In this review, we discuss different methods to engineer tunable free energy landscapes for nanoscale confinement of molecules. We first describe fabrication strategies and static nanofluidic geometries, emphasizing how top-down nanotopographies impose equilibrium molecular conformations. We then examine mechanically and pneumatically tunable platforms that modulate confinement after fabrication, followed by more tunable field-based approaches that use electrokinetic, thermophoretic, optical, and plasmonic effects to localize, concentrate, and manipulate molecules in solution. Finally, we discuss emerging strategies that combine lithographically defined nanofluidic arrays with externally applied fields to create reversible and dynamically tunable confinement landscapes. Such approaches point toward a new generation of nanofluidic devices in which single molecules can be immobilized, released, and driven between conformational states in real time, enabling high-throughput studies of non-equilibrium biomolecular dynamics and active molecular control on chip.

item.title: What makes a laboratory self-driving? Mapping the SDL terminology landscape and introducing the FLEx categorization framework
item.description: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are increasingly used to accelerate experimentation across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, and related fields. Yet, the rapid development of autonomous experimentation has produced a fragmented terminology landscape in which overlapping terms, including autonomous laboratories, materials acceleration platforms, and robot scientists, are applied inconsistently. This complicates comparisons between systems and obscures what constitutes scientific autonomy. Here, we examine the definitions, historical development, disciplinary associations, and usage patterns of SDLs and related concepts. We further review existing approaches to categorizing autonomous laboratory systems and show that many rely on characteristics such as hardware complexity, system architecture, or human involvement that are difficult to apply consistently across disciplines and technologies. To provide a technology-independent alternative, we introduce the Feedback Loop Extent (FLEx) framework. FLEx classifies systems according to how far experimental feedback reaches into the scientific process, progressing from scripted execution without a scientific feedback loop to parameter optimization, autonomous experiment planning, hypothesis formulation, and scientific goal formulation. Applying FLEx to representative published systems shows that most contemporary SDLs autonomously plan experiments within human-defined objectives, whereas few demonstrably formulate hypotheses and none unambiguously reformulate broader scientific goals. FLEx provides a common language for distinguishing automation from different forms of autonomy and enables more transparent comparison and reporting of current and future SDLs.

item.title: Configuration-dependent hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics on S-doped RuO2(110): A first-principles study
item.description: Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a promising non-platinum electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet its intrinsic activity is limited by strong hydrogen adsorption on coordinatively unsaturated Ru surface sites.Density functional theory calculations show that substitutional sulfur doping improves the HER adsorption thermodynamics of RuO2(110) by tuning hydrogen adsorption via local environment engineering. S doping weakens excessive hydrogen binding and drives the system toward near-optimal HER thermodynamics, approaching the benchmark ΔGH of Pt[3]. Symmetry-based enumeration and energetic screening were used to construct 86 inequivalent S-doped RuO2(110) models, from which four thermodynamically accessible configurations with favorable hydrogen adsorption were identified. The results reveal that dopant concentration governs the thermodynamic accessibility of S-doped configurations, whereas the local atomic configuration around the Ru active sites determines the hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics within the accessible concentration window. Among the accessible motifs, the 2S-top H adsorption site (H on the Ru adjacent to a single S dopant) is the most favorable, with ΔGH ≈ 0.06 eV, essentially equal to the 1S-top site (0.06 eV). Electronic structure analysis shows that S-induced hybridization between Ru 4d and dopant-derived p states leads to a downward shift of the Ru d-band center and reduced charge localization, tuning the hydrogen adsorption free energy from −0.26 eV on pristine RuO2 to approximately 0.06 eV.

item.title: Multigram Synthesis of the 1,3-Substituted Cuneane Amino Acids
item.description: Cuneanes are obtained from cubanes in a single step and reproduce the exit vectors of meta- and parasubstituted benzenes, but the corresponding amino acid building blocks have remained unavailable. Herein, we report a preparative route to cuneane amino acids based on the Curtius rearrangement of cuneane halfesters. Both regioisomers of the 1,3-disubstituted series are accessible from the two complementary halfesters: tert-butanol gives the Boc-protected amino esters in 84% and 91% yield on a 10 g scale, and standard operations convert them into the Boc and Fmoc amino acids, the methyl and tert-butyl esters, and the corresponding amine hydrochlorides in 55-99% yield. In the 2,6-disubstituted series, the deprotected amine opens the cage: acidic removal of the Boc group gives the known ring-opened ketone, and removal of an allyl carbamate under neutral Pd(0) conditions gives the same ketone in 55% yield. Carrying out that removal in the presence of an active ester acylates the amine as it forms and delivers the benzamide in 54% yield.

item.title: Light-Induced Synthesis of Ultra Thick Polymer Brush Coatings with Boosted Antifogging Properties
item.description: Polymer brushes with thicknesses exceeding 500 nm are synthetically challenging and rarely reported, while their applications remain largely unexplored. A range of applications, including catalytic, antifriction, and antifogging/antifreezing surfaces, could greatly benefit from their highly packed and extended conformation. Very recently, ultra-thick (200–3000 nm) polymer brushes have been demonstrated with largely improved wear bearing in antifriction tests. Herein, we demonstrate eosin Y-mediated SI-PhotoATRP to generate poly(oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether)methacrylate (POEGMEMA) brushes up to 800 nm thick, easily tunable with green-light intensity. The series of polymer brushes ranging from 30 to 800 nm were systematically tested against fogging under cooling. The developed testing setup enabled detection of dew points, whose 2 shifts were most significant for the thickest POEGMEMA brushes, with a striking shift of 9 °C at 0.5 °C∙min−1. The analysis at different cooling rates enabled the decoupling of kinetic and thermodynamic components of the antifogging of polymer brushes for the first time. Our work exemplifies a synthetic route toward generation of ultra-thick polymer brushes and strongly supports their need for further structure-property relationship studies and potential applications.

item.title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts
Linear-Algebraic Audit of Biomedical Matrices: Five Empirical Case Studies in Regularized Inference
item.description: High-throughput biomedical assays—ranging from gene expression microarrays to mass spectrometry and clinical registries—routinely exhibit severe rank deficiency (N ≪ P ), zero-inflation, and extreme sample outliers. Standard chemometric and bioinformatics pipelines apply variance auto-scaling, simplex normalization, and bilinear projections (PCA/PLS-DA) without verifying operator conditioning or modal localization. Grounded in inverse problem theory, this empirical study subjects five public biomedical datasets to a sequential four-step linear-algebraic audit evaluating residual Gram conditioning (κ), Effective Degrees of Freedom (DoF), singular spectra (Σ), and Participation Ratios (PR). Across five empirical regimes—Golub leukemia microarrays (72×7129), a large-scale oncology cohort (1545×10935), zero-inflated NCI Arcene mass spectra (200 × 10000), Pomeroy central nervous system tumor profiles (60 × 7129), and the Cleveland cardiology registry (270 × 13)—we demonstrate how uncalibrated preprocessing inflates background noise threefold, collapses leading components onto fewer than 7 outlier samples, and bends multi-batch artifacts into parabolic horseshoes. Removing just 0.6 percent of leverage outliers identified by PR restores sample coherence nearly ninety-fold (PR : 6.4 → 548.1), providing a rigorous diagnostic standard for biomedical data hygiene.

item.title: Towards a Metrological Validation of PFAS Property Predictions by In-Context LLMs Across Four Architectures
item.description: In recent years, the use of large-language models (LLMs) as prediction tools has become increasingly popular. Despite this popularity, the metrological validation of LLMs in the study of chemical problems has been somehow neglected to date. To illustrate this need in chemistry, we introduce a minimal, metrologically grounded framework for validating in-context learning (ICL)-based prediction in LLMs on molecular physicochemical properties with reliable estimation of uncertainty. Our framework integrates a multicycle testing protocol (Mc = 50 replicate cycles per model-property cell) with a six-metric bundle: central tendency (mean MAE over replicate cycles), reproducibility (interquartile range), regression performance (RMSE, and R2), information-theoretical lower bound on the amount of captured signal (𝐼" in nats), and ordinal 2 performance (accuracy against the median in the dataset), plus three cross-property and crossmodel comparison metrics: NRMSE, Welch’s z-test, and Scaling Law Fit exponents. We use this framework to validate four LLMs, two dense (8B and 70B parameters; 1B = 109) and two mixture-of-experts (MoE; 17B active parameters with 109B and 400B in total), for predicting eight per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) properties: boiling point (BP), melting point (MP), vapor pressure (VP), Henry’s law constant (HLC), octanol-water partition coefficient (LogKow), aqueous solubility (LogS), acid dissociation constant (pKa), and critical micelle concentration (LogCMC). In this benchmark, the frontier MoE model (Maverick 400B parameters) achieves a mean validation NRMSE of 14.4 %, and the mid-scale MoE model (Scout, 109B parameters) outperforms our larger dense model (Llama-3.3-70B) despite having 4.1× fewer active parameters. This suggests that MoE routed capacity can substitute for activeparameter scale in chemical applications of ICL. When compared to published QSPR and DFT baselines, LLM-ICL beats these approaches on three of eight directly comparable properties (pKa by 43 %, LogKow by 31 %, HLC by 10 %) and trails behind on five (BP, MP, LogS, VP by 12 % to 75 %, and LogCMC by a factor of approx. 3.3), despite using approximately 32 incontext examples (32 for seven properties, 20 for HLC) versus the training sets comprising 102 to 105 molecules used in these approaches. We also discuss a validation-set anomaly in the case of LogKow, where our mid-scale dense model Llama-3.3-70B outperforms the frontier MoE model on all four validation metrics, possibly due to better coverage of the pretraining data. Permutation (shuffled-label) and information-access blinding controls show that genuine structure-response signal is present, but that the native-prompt accuracy depends substantially on pretrained, property-specific knowledge and familiar target scales. Overall, our results suggest a two-fold conclusion on the competitiveness of LLM-ICL: it succeeds in predicting chemical

item.title: Self-Consistent Induced Dipoles for MACE-POLAR in Molecular Embedding and Classical Dynamics
item.description: We couple the native Gaussian multipoles of MACE-POLAR-1-M to classical induced dipoles and compare the resulting solute densities, fields and forces with quantum references. The density-driven fixed point has a nonzero energy derivative with respect to its dipoles. An adjoint recovers forces on the converged surface to within 2.13 × 10−7 eV/Å of reconverged finite differences in twelve force-test configurations. A separate density comparison treats both partners quantum mechanically at twelve geometries of six small complexes. At a common Gaussian width of 1.5 Å, enabling mutual induction changes the native MACE solute density by at most 6.81 × 10−4 𝑒 in integrated absolute difference. For water facing chloride at 3.15 Å, the density change is 0.000107 𝑒 with the MACE-induced dipole, 0.00426 𝑒 with the prescribed DFT-induced dipole, and 0.01026 𝑒 with DFT at that same dipole. Thus the error involves both the field that induces chloride and the water response to the returning field. For Na+–Ar at 6 Å, the predicted solute multipoles are unchanged, while environment induction gives an interaction of −9.19 meV, close to the classical induction limit

item.title: AMBER2LAMMPS: Validated conversion of AMBER-family topologies to LAMMPS
item.description: AMBER topology files encode a complete molecular-mechanics model rather than only molecular connectivity. Translating them to LAMMPS requires preservation of bonded parameters, charges, Lennard-Jones coefficients, exclusions, topology-specific 1–4 scaling, masses, and periodic-cell semantics. AMBER2LAMMPS is an open-source Python package that converts one or more fully parameterized AMBER topology templates and matching PDB coordinates to LAMMPS data and parameter files. The converter derives SCEE and SCNB scaling from active proper dihedrals, represents non-covalent GAFF2–GLYCAM mixtures with repeated hybrid pair-style instances, supports validated ff14SB, TIP3P, ion, and Li/Merz 12–6–4 cases, plus HMR mass mapping and TIP3P SHAKE initialization, and fails before output for unsupported combinations. Reproducible continuous-integration fixtures compare component energies and every Cartesian force against AmberTools sander. A command-line interface, Python API, and bounded Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface, with optional (CLI) or automatic (MCP) provenance, support both manual and automated workflows while keeping scientific decisions inspectable.

item.title: Informatics-Driven Chemputation within the HERA Framework: Mathematical Modeling of Molecular State Entropy, Reaction-Diffusion Flow Kinetics, and Closed-Loop Bayesian Optimization
item.description: The integration of physical chemical synthesis with digital information networks remains bottlenecked by the lack of unified frameworks for lossless molecular state serialization, secure long-range telemetry, and automated robotic re-materialization. This study introduces the HERA framework, a comprehensive model that converts chemical supply chains into executable digital information routing problems. We establish a rigorous information-theoretic foundation by defining total chemical state information entropy H(C) as a decomposition of structural discrete entropy (H_struct), thermodynamic vibrational entropy (H_vib), and compositional concentration entropy (H_conc). To bypass intractable high-scaling quantum mechanical calculations (O(N⁷) Coupled Cluster theory), we formulate Graph Neural Network (GNN) surrogate operators (H_GNN) that reduce computational complexity to O(N²) while bounding prediction error within ε_q <= 10⁷Hartree. Furthermore, we derive lossless HERA Data Container (HDC) compression bounds, reaction-diffusion transport kinetic partial differential equations governed by the Peclet number for continuous-flow Chemical Processing Units (ChemPUs), and Kullback-Leibler (D_KL) spectral divergence thresholds to enforce hardware safety and error-correction. Grounded in open analytical standards (mzML, nmrML, AnIML), chemoinformatics serialization (InChI, RInChI, xDL), and closed-loop Bayesian optimization within self-driving laboratories, HERA establishes a secure, dual-use protected pathway for decentralized pharmaceutical manufacturing, hazardous forensics, and deep-space astropharmacy.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: QM/MM Simulations Reveal Differences in Hydrolysis Mechanisms of Ertapenem and Faropenem in L1 Metallo-β-Lactamase Leading to Different Product Binding Modes
item.description: L1, a class B3 metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) from Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, efficiently hydrolyzes most β-lactam antibiotics and evades β-lactamase inhibitors, both clinically available and those in late-stage trials targeting other MBLs. Detailed understanding of the L1 mechanism is necessary to design effective inhibitors. Building on our previous quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) study of L1catalyzed hydrolysis of the penem antibiotic faropenem, we here investigate hydrolysis of a 1β-methyl carbapenem (ertapenem) using MM and enhanced sampling QM/MM MD simulations at the DFTB3 level, comparing the two mechanisms to understand the distinct product binding modes observed crystallographically. The geometry of the transition state for the first, amide bond cleavage, reaction step is similar for both substrates. However, differences are apparent in the subsequent proton transfer step, corresponding to the different binding modes observed crystallographically for the respective products. For faropenem, a bulk water molecule enters the active site, yielding the (2S )-imine-∆1 product via rotation about the C5–C6 bond and protonation at position C2. For ertapenem, the metal-bridging hydroxide is the proton source, and the equivalent rotation is associated with a relatively high barrier. Instead, the more favorable rotation of the C6-carboxyl enables protonation at C2, yielding the (2S )-imine-∆1 product in a distinct binding mode. Long-timescale MM MD simulations indicate rapid dissociation of the ertapenem-derived imine, compared to the faropenem-derived species, from the L1 active site, offering insight into the relative stability of these binding modes. These data reveal how carbapenem and MBL structure influence hydrolysis pathways, and may inform rational MBL inhibitor design.

item.title: A Convenient One-Pot Route to [Thianthrenium][B(C6F5)4]
item.description: One-electron oxidants paired with weakly coordinating anions are indispensable for accessing reactive cations. The thianthrenium radical cation, [TA]•+ (TA = thianthrene), is a strong outer-sphere oxidant (E1/2 ≈ +0.8 V vs ferrocene/ferrocenium) whose neutral by-product is easily removed, and its [B(C6F5)4]− salt (1) has been used in organometallic, rare-earth, and porphyrin chemistry. Existing preparations often rely on nitrosonium oxidation or salt metathesis in liquid SO2, which is challenging to handle, or MeCN, where traces may be deleterious to subsequent reaction steps. Here, 1 is obtained in one step at room temperature from AgI[B(C6F5)4], TA and 0.5 equivalents of I2 in CH2Cl2 or fluorobenzene; AgII is removed by filtration, and crystalline 1·CH2Cl2 and 1·0.5C6H5F are isolated in high yield on a gram scale.

item.title: Correlative Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy and Nano-DESI Mass Spectrometry Imaging for Mapping Isomeric Triglycerides in Lipid Droplets in Biological Tissues
item.description: Lipid droplets (LDs) are key organelles involved in lipid storage and metabolic regulation. Triglycerides (TGs) are the major component of LDs’ neutral lipid core. Alterations in TG composition are associated with different biological states or disease conditions, yet spatially resolved analysis of TG isomers in biological tissues remains challenging. Here, we present a correlative multimodal imaging strategy that integrates stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy with high-resolution nanospray desorption electrospray ionization (nano-DESI) isomer selective mass spectrometry imaging (iMSI) to map LD morphology and isomeric TG distributions in biological tissues. We performed SRS imaging on a type 2 diabetes (T2D) mouse liver tissue section to visualize individual LDs with sub-micron resolution and without the need of labeling. We then performed nano-DESI iMSI on the same tissue section. By optimizing nano-DESI solvent composition and tissue preparation conditions to favor formation of ammonium adducts of TGs, [M+NH4]+, we obtained simplified, isomer-selective MS2 fragmentation patterns revealing characteristic fatty acyl neutral losses. We then used these characteristic fragment ions to perform high-resolution iMSI of four TG species (TG 50:2, TG 50:3, TG 52:2, and TG 52:3) and map the spatial distributions of their isomers. Spatial correlation analysis across defined regions of interest demonstrated consistent signal trends between SRS-derived LD density and MSI TG ion signal, with both modalities showing minimal signal in blood vessel regions and elevated signals in LD-rich areas. This first demonstration of iMSI of TGs in biological tissues provides a framework for correlative SRS-MSI imaging of LDs and TG isomers in metabolic disease models.

item.title: Direct Access to 5-Aryl-2-Pyrones via Palladium-Catalyzed Decarbonylative Cross-Coupling of Coumalic Acid
item.description: The selective synthesis of 5-substituted 2-pyrones remains challenging despite their synthetic potential. Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed decarbonylative Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling of simple coumalic acid, providing direct access to 5aryl-2-pyrones in up to 58% yield. Enabled by DPEphos, the transformation accommodates diverse arylboronic acids while preserving the reactive heterocyclic framework. Subsequent cycloaddition chemistry exploits the localized diene motif to furnish stereodefined cyclohexenes and highly substituted arenes, highlighting their versatility as synthetic building blocks.

item.title: Benzylsuccinate synthase as an engineerable platform for stereoselective C–C bond formation via C–H functionalization
item.description: Stereoselective olefin hydroalkylation offers a direct route to chiral C(sp3)-rich products from simple C–H substrates, but biocatalytic platforms for this transformation are rare. Glycyl radical enzymes catalyze hydroalkylation in anaerobic metabolism, yet applications in chemical synthesis have been precluded by a lack of methods for in vitro activation. Here we use a soluble activase to unlock GRE hydroalkylases as a tunable class of radical biocatalysts. We demonstrate broad substrate scope, high stereocontrol, and preparative-scale utility, while showing through systematic mutagenesis that 17 of 18 active-site residues can be altered without loss of activity. Variants expand reactivity and alter regioselectivity. Structural analysis reveals how mutagenesis improves turnover. These results transform GRE hydroalkylases from pathway-specific metabolic enzymes into engineerable catalysts for stereocontrolled C–C bond formation.

item.title: Exploring Boltzmann Distributions via Kernel-Based Fokker–Planck Ensemble Transport
item.description: Local trajectory-based samplers can relax within a visited basin long before finite trajectories cross barriers to other Boltzmann-relevant regions. We introduce the Fokker–Planck Transformer (FPT), a training-free interacting-ensemble method that makes the instantaneous ensemble distribution a dynamical variable, shifting exploration from trajectory-wise barrier crossing toward distribution-level redistribution. FPT discretizes the current-velocity representation of overdamped Fokker–Planck evolution by combining energetic drift with a kernel estimate of the ensemble score. The continuum flow has the Boltzmann density as its stationary target and monotonically dissipates configurational free energy and relative entropy. A Gaussian row-mass selector couples increasing local occupancy to a vanishing spatial scale without a separate bandwidth limit. For its fresh explicit-Euler realization, pathwise score residuals propagate to distributional and observable errors, while a weak-flux argument gives conditional fixed-horizon convergence to the Fokker–Planck solution. For this realization, a controlled two-dimensional calculation tracks transport from a localized Gaussian toward equilibrium against a numerically propagated Fokker–Planck reference. In a three-dimensional periodic landscape, an exact Fokker–Planck reference shows that a shared-bandwidth approximation populates distant wells far ahead of the continuum solution, which accounts for its faster support discovery; the transported ensemble runs warm, and a Hastings-corrected continuation from its endpoint restores the energy distribution within two steps. Further tests in a 100-dimensional landscape, alanine decapeptide, and 190 docking systems show rapid expansion of Boltzmann-relevant support, with the clearest gains over matched local controls when barriers or configurational complexity limit global exploration. Overall, FPT provides thermodynamically grounded finite-budget support discovery and can seed target-preserving sampling.

item.title: Two-carbon annulation of primary amines to azetidines
item.description: Azetidines are valuable motifs in medicinal chemistry, yet their broader use is constrained by a lack of general, concise methods for preparing N–H azetidines from simple feedstocks. Here, we report a direct two-carbon annulation of unprotected primary alkylamines that provides α-mono- and α,α-disubstituted azetidines. Dual photoredox and hydrogen-atomtransfer catalysis enables α-C–H alkylation with vinylsulfonium reagents to generate γ-amino sulfonium intermediates, which undergo intramolecular SN2 cyclization to forge the fourmembered ring without protecting groups or prefunctionalization. Low-temperature continuous flow is critical for overriding the innate N-centered reactivity of primary amines and suppressing rapid N-alkylation by the vinylsulfonium reagent. The method uses commercially available building blocks, tolerates a range of functional groups, and provides streamlined access to azetidines that are otherwise challenging to prepare. Successful kilogram-scale translation, underpinned by process-safety assessment, demonstrates that the low-temperature flow strategy is transferable beyond discovery scale.
